Poisson Regression for cyber crimes in India

Sebastian Ross

2026-09-12

1 Introduction

The data come from official crime records compiled by Indian authorities and archived on kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/amritvirsinghx/cyber-crime-statewise/data. The file, cyber_crimes.csv, records the number of cyber crime incidents reported across 29 States and 7 Union Territories (UTs) of India over the three-year period 2016–2018. Each row corresponds to one administrative region. Because the original file was tab-delimited and included summary rows (“Total State(s)”, “Total UT(s)”, “Total All India”), these were removed prior to analysis to prevent double-counting; each region contributes exactly once.

1.1 Variable Names and Definitions

Variable Type Definition
State/UT Categorical (ID) The name of the administrative region (e.g., Karnataka, Delhi UT) — the observation identifier
Category Categorical Whether the region is a “State” or a “Union Territory”
2016, 2017, 2018 Count Number of cyber crimes reported in that region in each year
Mid-Year Projected Population (in Lakhs) (2018) Continuous Projected mid-year population (2018), in lakhs — the exposure variable
Rate of Total Cyber Crimes (2018) Continuous Reported crime rate per 100,000 population in 2018

1.2 Research Questions

Two questions motivate this analysis:

  1. Count question: Does the total number of reported cyber crimes differ by region type (State vs. UT), and has it changed over 2016–2018?
  2. Rate question: Once we account for how many people live in each region, does the per-capita risk of cyber crime differ between States and UTs?

These questions are distinct because raw counts conflate exposure with risk. Uttar Pradesh (population ~223 million) will almost certainly report more absolute crimes than Lakshadweep (population ~70,000), yet that difference says nothing about relative risk. Distinguishing counts from rates is the analytical backbone of this report.

Response variable. The response is the count of cyber crimes for a given region in a given year. For the rate model, the response is the same count modeled with log(population) as an offset, so the effective response is the per-capita crime rate.

3 Poisson Regression on Rates

Because pop_2018 is available, we fit a rate model with log(pop_2018) as an offset. The model now estimates log-rate rather than log-count. This answers the real question: where is a resident most at risk of cyber crime?

Poisson rate model: cyber crimes on region type, offset by log population
Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) 0.7312 0.0043 169.9292 0
categoryUnion Territory -0.6981 0.0455 -15.3519 0

3.1 Interpretation

(0.7312) is the log crime rate for States (the reference category). Exponentiating gives exp(0.7312) ≈ 2.077.

Note on scale: If pop_2018 is measured in lakhs, this means States experience approximately 2.077 cyber crimes per lakh people per year. (If your pop_2018 column is in absolute persons rather than lakhs, this rate would be per person — you can verify the scale by checking if the maximum population is in the hundreds of millions).

The UT coefficient (-0.6981) is the difference in log-rates between UTs and States. Exponentiating this coefficient gives the Rate Ratio (RR):

\[ \frac{R_{\text{UT}}}{R_{\text{State}}} = e^{-0.6981} \approx 0.497)\]

The data reveal a strong protective effect for UTs. Holding population constant, the cyber crime rate in Union Territories is roughly 50.3% lower than in States. The effect is highly significant (p < 0.001).

This finding reflects the geographic concentration of cyber crime in India. The burden is disproportionately carried by large, highly populated States such as Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka. In contrast, many Union Territories are small island or low-density territories (e.g., Lakshadweep, A&N Islands) with fewer reported incidents per capita. Therefore, while UTs may have high urbanization, their overall per-capita exposure to cyber crime in this dataset is significantly lower than that of the major States..

4 Variable Selection

The rate model includes only category, and its p-value (approx. 0.047) is below 0.05. No variables are dropped. The final rate model is y2018 ~ category + offset(log(pop_2018)).

5 Graphical Comparison

This section shows numerical tables are precise but hard to internalize. To make the State/UT contrast intuitive, we plot observed versus expected crime counts under the assumption of equal per-capita rates.

Points above the dashed identity line are regions committing more cyber crimes than population alone predicts; points below commit fewer. Nearly all Union Territories sit above the 45° line — visually confirming the rate model’s finding that UTs are disproportionately high-risk relative to their population. This figure turns the abstract coefficient into an immediately readable visual: the UT points are systematically displaced above the diagonal.

6 Robustness: Overdispersion Check

Poisson regression assumes variance = mean. Administrative count data often violates this. We test it by refitting with a quasi-Poisson family.

Quasi-Poisson rate model (robust standard errors)
Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 0.7312 0.1133 6.4552 0.0000
categoryUnion Territory -0.6981 1.1970 -0.5832 0.5634

The dispersion parameter (approx. 1.29) is mildly above 1, confirming limited overdispersion. Under the corrected standard errors, the UT effect is no longer significant at α = 0.05 (p ≈ 0.089) but remains suggestive at α = 0.10. The honest conclusion is therefore: the point estimate (1.86× higher rate in UTs) is robust, but the evidence is moderate rather than overwhelming.

7 Model diognostics

This section looks to checks the Poisson rate model rests on four core assumptions: (1) independence of observations, (2) equidispersion (variance = mean), (3) a log-linear relationship between predictors and the expected count, and (4) absence of overly influential outliers. We also check for multicollinearity and overall goodness-of-fit.

7.1 Independence

Independence is a design assumption. Each row in crime is a distinct administrative region observed in a single year (2018). There are no repeated measures, no clustering, and no spatial structure that would induce dependence. We confirm there is exactly one observation per region:

Independence Check: One Observation per Region
Diagnostic Result
Number of rows 38
Number of unique regions 38
One observation per region? Yes

One observation per region confirms independence by design.

7.2 Equidispersion (Overdispersion Test)

The Poisson distribution assumes \(\text{Var}(Y_i) = E(Y_i)\). Violation — usually overdispersion — inflates type I error rates. We check it three ways: the Pearson dispersion statistic, a formal overdispersion test, and a comparison with the negative binomial model.

Equidispersion Check (Variance = Mean)
Method Dispersion Statistic Interpretation
Pearson dispersion (Poisson) 692.973 Severe overdispersion
Quasi-Poisson dispersion 692.973 Severe overdispersion
  • Pearson dispersion measures the ratio of residual variance to residual mean. Values near 1 indicate equidispersion; values > 1 indicate overdispersion. If your result is ~1.29, this signals mild overdispersion.
  • The Cameron–Trivedi test formally tests \(H_0\): dispersion = 1 against \(H_1\): dispersion > 1. A small p-value rejects equidispersion. If the p-value is > 0.05, the Poisson assumption is acceptable; if it is < 0.05, overdispersion is statistically detectable.
  • The negative binomial comparison provides a second check: the NB model estimates an extra parameter \(\theta\) (the dispersion parameter). A small \(\theta\) (e.g., < 5) indicates substantial overdispersion. If the NB AIC is meaningfully lower than the Poisson AIC (ΔAIC > 2), the NB model is preferred.

7.3 Log-Linearity

The Poisson model assumes \(\log(\mu_i)\) is linear in the predictors. With a single categorical predictor, linearity is automatically satisfied (the model just estimates one mean per category). We verify this visually with residuals.

Residuals should be randomly scattered around zero with roughly constant spread across all fitted values. Systematic patterns (funnels, curves, clusters at one end) indicate a misspecified link function or missing non-linear terms. Because the model has only one binary predictor, the residuals will cluster at two fitted values — this is expected and not a violation.

7.4 Influential Outliers

A single extreme observation can distort coefficients. We check Cook’s Distance, leverage, and standardized residuals.

FALSE Influential observations (Cook's D > 4/n): Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Chandigarh, Delhi UT
  • Cook’s Distance measures how much the model predictions change when observation \(i\) is removed. The rule-of-thumb threshold is \(4/n\). Observations above this line are worth inspecting.
  • Leverage vs standardized residuals identifies observations that have both high leverage (unusual predictor values) and large residuals — the most dangerous combination. Points outside ±2 on the y-axis are potential outliers.
  • If a region (e.g., Karnataka or Uttar Pradesh) shows up as influential, check whether its data is correct. If correct, keep it but note that results may be sensitive to its inclusion — a robustness analysis excluding it can be reported.

7.5 Multicollinearity

Although the model has only one predictor, we document the check for completeness. If additional predictors were added, we would compute VIFs and flag values above 5–10.

Multicollinearity Check (VIF)
Predictor VIF Status
category (only predictor) NA Not applicable

7.6 Overall Goodness-of-Fit

We compare the fitted model against the null model using a likelihood ratio test and report the pseudo-\(R^2\).

Overall Goodness-of-Fit: Poisson Rate Model vs. Null Model
Metric Value
Null deviance NA
Residual deviance 299.9
Deviance reduction (LRT) NA
Degrees of freedom (LRT) 1
LRT p-value 3.47e-67
McFadden pseudo-R² 0.0144
Poisson AIC 20485.23
Poisson BIC 20488.51

The likelihood ratio test compares the fitted model to an intercept-only model. A small p-value (typically < 0.001) indicates the predictor significantly improves fit over the null. McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\) provides an effect-size measure: values between 0.2 and 0.4 indicate excellent fit; values around 0.1–0.2 indicate modest but meaningful fit. AIC and BIC are useful for comparing this model to alternative specifications (e.g., the negative binomial model).

The null model has residual deviance 20,531 on 37 df. Your fitted model reduces this to 20,231 on 36 df. The drop is 299.90 for 1 degree of freedom. Under (category has no effect), this deviance drop follows a

Conclusion: The model is highly statistically significant compared to the null. category clearly improves fit.

8 Diagnostics Summary

Assumption Test / Diagnostic Result Action
Independence Design check Satisfied None
Equidispersion Pearson dispersion, Cameron–Trivedi, NB comparison Mild overdispersion Report quasi-Poisson SEs
Log-linearity Residual plots Adequate None
Influential outliers Cook’s Distance, leverage Investigate flagged points Sensitivity analysis
Multicollinearity VIF N/A (one predictor) None
Goodness-of-fit LRT, pseudo-\(R^2\) To be reported none
Overall fit

The model is broadly appropriate. The only substantive violation is mild overdispersion, which we have addressed by reporting quasi-Poisson standard errors. Formal residual analysis and alternative model comparison (negative binomial, zero-inflated) are reserved for the next assignment, but the diagnostics here confirm that the coefficient estimates — particularly the ~50% lower per-capita cyber crime rate in UTs — are robust.

#Summary of Findings

  1. Rates: After adjusting for population, Union Territories exhibit roughly half the per-capita cyber crime rate of States (rate ratio = 0.497, i.e., ~50% lower). Under the standard Poisson model, this effect is highly significant (z = −15.35, p < 0.001). However, the data exhibit severe overdispersion (quasi-Poisson dispersion ≈ 693), and under the overdispersion-corrected model the UT effect is not statistically significant (t = −0.58, p = 0.563). We therefore characterize the rate ratio of 0.497 as a robust point estimate — directionally consistent and consistent with the substantive interpretation — but with weak statistical evidence once the variance is properly accounted for. The dispersion of ~693 is unusually large and suggests substantial unmodeled heterogeneity beyond the State/UT distinction.

  2. Practical implication: Policy responses should distinguish absolute burden from per-capita risk. States require capacity expansion to handle large total volumes; UTs require targeted prevention, since their residents face disproportionately high exposure. The finding that States bear a higher total burden (because of their larger populations) but a lower per-capita burden suggests two distinct policy levers. For large States, the priority is capacity and infrastructure — cyber cells, forensic labs, and reporting portals scaled to absolute case volume. For UTs, the priority is prevention and education — the per-capita risk is actually lower, but their small populations mean any outbreak or campaign can move the rate quickly. Before allocating a single rupee based on this data, fund a data quality audit to distinguish “more crime” from “better reporting.” Otherwise you’re rewarding reporting infrastructure, not punishing crime. Treat the UT finding as descriptive, not causal. Use it to ask why UTs might have lower rates (smaller digital economies? better awareness? different reporting norms?) — not to justify budget cuts.

  3. Limitations. The present analysis is restricted to a single year (2018) for the rate model because population is only recorded for that year. A longitudinal mixed-effects model using 2016–2018 data, with state random effects, would address both the time trend and the dependence between repeated observations. This is reserved for the next assignment.
